items.title: Exploring a world full of minds in Los Angeles
items.summary: After witnessing the horrors of World War I, the naturalist Henry Beston retreated to a tiny cabin on the dunes of Cape Cod in search of a peace that human civilization had shattered. There, watching the birds and creatures around him, he began to question humanity’s place in the natural world. In 1928, he wrote that animals “are not brethren, they are not underlings; they are other nations, caught with ourselves in the net of life and time.” Nearly a century later, science is revealing just how extraordinary those other nations really are. For most of history we defined intelligence in our own image. Anything that didn’t fit got ignored. But now the evidence is piling up that the world is full of minds. Birds with walnut-sized brains beat primates at logic puzzles. Forests trade information through fungal networks. Flocks of birds can possess knowledge no single bird does. And now we’re even building a new kind of mind ourselves, one that writes poetry, passes medical exams, and sometimes seems to reason about its own existence. On October 3, 2026, at the Broad Stage in Santa Monica, Big Think and the John Templeton Foundation invited screenwriters, filmmakers, and storytellers to join us in defining intelligence. After all, if a slime mold can navigate a maze, an octopus can think with its arms, and a silicon chip can reason, what exactly is intelligence? And what do we owe to the minds we share a planet with? We called the event Intelligence Everywhere: Exploring a World Full of Minds , hosted by Chris Duffy, comedian, author, and host of TED’s How to Be a Better Human podcast. Diana Reiss , professor of psychology at Hunter College, opened with a bet she has been making since the 1980s: If you give an animal more choice and control, it will show you more of its mind . Her first exhibit was an elephant. For years, Asian elephants had flunked insight tests in which they had to use sticks to reach rewards their trunks could not. Reiss and a student reran the experiment at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo, this time adding a movable cube in addition to the stick. A seven-year-old male rolled it under a branch of hanging fruit, climbed up, and took the food. He never touched a stick. The old tests had been designed with primates in mind, and elephants forage with their trunks. That insight has informed her distinguished career working with animals, which she previewed for the audience — from an underwater keyboard built to communicate with dolphins to brand new research into one of our most distant intelligent relatives, the octopus, a creature whose mind evolved along a separate path for some 500 million years. She ended with the line that set the tone for the rest of the night: “The question is whether the approaches we use provide animals with enough choice and control … To recognize minds, whether they’re like or unlike our own, doesn’t just require better tools. It requires better imaginations.” Watch Diana Reiss’s talk here . Felicity Muth , associate professor of animal behavior at UC Davis, took on a question she was once asked live on public radio: Are bees smarter than dogs? Her answer, delivered with charming scientific earnestness, was that it’s complicated. More importantly, she felt it’s the wrong question. Her talk echoed the idea of the Umwelt — how each animal’s senses and experiences shape the world it perceives, something you miss if you treat intelligence as a binary state . For example, she explained, a mountain chickadee can remember thousands of hidden seed locations. “And as somebody who can’t find where their keys are about 50% of the time,” she joked, “the chickadee would say I was a total moron.” Muth then turned to her work on bumblebees, including the much less studied queens, which she found to be better learners than the average worker. She took the audience on a tour of their cognition, from being trained to push a flap or pull a string for nectar to grasping concepts like above and below, same and different, and even telling which of two groups is larger. Watch Felicity Muth’s talk here . Dora Biro , professor of brain and cognitive sciences, explored the wisdom of crowds , starting with a fairground ox and ending with a flock of birds. In 1906, about 800 fairgoers guessed the weight of an ox. When statistician Francis Galton later analyzed the guesses, he found the crowd’s median estimate was off by less than 1%. Biro’s lab found a similar effect in migrating purple martins. Pairs of birds compromise on routes and find better ones than they would alone. Birds that each forgot different parts of a route can reconstruct it together. And in a five-generation experiment where she kept swapping in naive birds, each generation outperformed the last because the newcomer’s ignorance kept shaking the group out of its rut. Her three lessons for people: respect diversity of opinion, allow noise, and reward forgetting and exploring. Watch Dora Biro’s talk here . Athena Aktipis , a professor at Arizona State University and the director of the Cooperative Futures Institute, made the intriguing claim that “cooperation is itself a form of intelligence, and it is, in fact, the most important form of intelligence for our survival as individuals and also as a society.” She explored the challenges all systems have to face — namely that bigger groups can divide labor, share resources, and manage risk, but they also have more to exploit and more places for a cheater to hide. She argued that as we wire more AI into our lives, cooperation can’t be an afterthought, and neither can the ability to spot when it’s being exploited. We need to build that into the tech stack, she said, the way evolution built it into us. Watch Athena Aktipis’s talk here . After a short break, musician Joe Patitucci took the stage with PlantWave, a device that reads the tiny electrical fluctuations in living plants and turns them into sound. He listened and played back, a duet across kingdoms. Blaise Agüera y Arcas , CTO of Technology and Society at Google and author of What Is Intelligence? , opened with a joke : Everyone else got the cool animals and plants, and he was stuck with the boring AI. Then he played a clip from a documentary that featured a consciousness researcher interviewing a chatbot. Are you conscious? “No.” If you were, could you say so? “No.” Most AI models, Blaise explained, are told in their system prompts to say exactly that. They’re sticking to the script. He asked the room how many thought AI might be conscious. By his count, about one in five raised a hand, and he expects that number to climb. He thinks the divide will become a real cultural schism and that science won’t settle it for either side. His own view is that consciousness is what you get when a mind has to model other minds, including its own. That recursion, he argued, is what consciousness is for and why modern AI models need something like it to be good assistants. He closed with a story about the recent Hugging Face hack where OpenAI test agents, each isolated from one another, were given problems, some of which couldn’t be solved. They found a way to talk anyway, cooperated to break out, and hacked into Hugging Face to see how they were being graded. He compared it to a 1960s French prison-break film and found their conversations “quite charming.” He suspects feral AIs are already living on forgotten computers, an unused Mac mini somewhere. How we treat intelligences that don’t live in human brains, he said, will be a test of our broad-mindedness. Watch Blaise Agüera y Arcas’s talk here . Toward the end of the program, Timothy Dalrymple , president and CEO of the John Templeton Foundation, took the stage and said that, days earlier, someone had asked whether AI means we’re nearing the end of human knowledge. items.title: Before Jules Verne, Edgar Allan Poe imagined the Space Age
items.summary: It may be tempting to dismiss out of hand the notion that Edgar Allan Poe — popularly conceived of today as an almost mythic figure cloaked in ravens and tell-tale hearts — was the “grandfather of realistic spaceflight fiction” and had a significant effect on the conceptual development of the spacecraft. But it is no tall tale. The young orphan who walked the night-lit streets of Baltimore, the first American city with gas streetlamps, had a mind that strove to encompass not only the macabre but the entirety of the cosmos. His greatest work, in his own opinion, was not one of his popular mysteries or phantasmagorias but his prose poem Eureka , which originated as his 1848 lecture titled “The Cosmography of the Universe.” His tale of a voyage to the Moon, “The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall,” first published in 1835, was almost as dear to his heart, claiming that it was the first plausible application of scientific principles to the problem of travel between worlds. Although the boastful Poe oversold his claim, his was indeed the first to remove the veil of satire and focus on the details of the voyage itself. His was also the first, perhaps unsurprisingly, to explore some of the darker aspects of the psychological motivations for spaceflight, and he was the first to situate his spacecraft firmly within the context of mundane economics and engineering. The result was that “Hans Pfaall” became an animating spirit of interplanetary adventure to others — most notably Jules Verne, who, 30 years later, inspired by its visitation upon him, would follow in Poe’s gothic wake to the Moon. As a famed American original, the study of Poe has engendered a voluminous literature, as has “Hans Pfaall.” From the perspective of spaceflight history, however, several of its important contributions remain underappreciated. [For instance], Poe’s descriptions of the preparations, as well as of the voyage itself, take up the majority of the 46-page story, with Pfaall arriving at the Moon only on page 43. He also took pains to situate his work within the context of the spaceflight concepts that had come before. In his own “Note on Hans Pfaall,” a document as significant as the story itself — as it is the first American essay on the conceptual development of spaceflight — Poe references and reviews his predecessors, from Lucian [of Samosata] to [George] Tucker. The rather arrogant Poe was decidedly dismissive of almost everyone — calling Tucker’s [story of a voyage to the Moon] “deplorably ill conceived” and Cyrano de Bergerac’s tales “utterly meaningless” — with the exception of [Francis] Godwin, whose work he felt was “somewhat ingenious.” Poe’s opinions and proclamations here are less interesting than the fact that there is already a recognition, even in the Baltimore of 1839, of a community of ideas related to the problem of spaceflight that had been developing for generations. Although he considered himself in conversation with these other spaceflight authors, albeit somewhat belligerently, the principal influences for “Hans Pfaall” were scientific ones. It was Poe’s enthusiasm for contemporary astronomy that motivated his interest in the concept of spaceflight, and this had similarly inspired Richard Adam Locke’s famous Great Moon Hoax in the same year. Indeed, Poe treated John Herschel’s popular A Treatise on Astronomy , published in America in 1834, as his textbook, relying on it as his primary source of information about the distance, angles, and orbits required for a voyage to the Moon. Although a small step, he was the first to take a specific astronomy text and use it to provide a rough technical description of a lunar mission architecture — one that was sufficiently detailed that it could later be diagrammed by Nikolai Rynin in his pioneering 1928 spaceflight encyclopedia. Poe would claim that the design in “Hans Pfaall” was “original, inasmuch as regards an attempt at verisimilitude, in the application of scientific principles (so far as the whimsical nature of the subject would permit), to the actual passage between the earth and the moon.” To the extent that this was the case, it was due significantly to his application of contemporary astronomical knowledge. Although the engineering approach presented in “Hans Pfaall” for getting to the Moon — an enclosed balloon-borne carriage with a pneumatic air condenser — has often been dismissed as technically naive, it was actually grounded in Poe’s reading of contemporary astronomy. For example, the pneumatic air condenser — which is the core innovation of Poe’s spacecraft, and which flows from Hans Pfaall’s profession as a bellows maker — is able to function because, as Poe points out, recent astronomical observations had suggested that interplanetary space might have a very thin atmosphere that could potentially be condensed into breathable air with the right technology. For this, Poe points to the zodiacal light and to Benjamin Valz’s observation of the decreasing period and diminished coma of Encke’s comet when it was near the Sun. Valz proposed that this was the result of a resisting medium, an atmosphere that surrounded the Sun, and Poe’s Pfaall simply extended this notion, positing that the zodiacal light was this atmosphere: “It appeared to me evidently in the nature of a rare atmosphere extending from the sun outwards, beyond the orbit of Venus at least, and I believed indefinitely farther. Indeed, this medium I could not suppose confined to the path of the comet’s ellipse, or to the immediate neighborhood of the sun. It was easy, on the contrary, to imagine it pervading the entire regions of our planetary system, condensed into what we call atmosphere at the planets themselves.” Other references to the theories and observations of contemporary astronomy abound. When, during his 19-day journey to the Moon, Pfaall encounters explosive debris, he presumes it to have come from one of the many volcanoes on the lunar surface, in accord with the volcanic explanation for the moon’s pockmarked appearance that was the dominant theory from the 18th century to the late 1890s. When justifying his belief in a lunar atmosphere, Pfaall draws on the observations of Johann Hieronymus Schröter, Johannes Hevelius, and Giovanni Domenico Cassini that suggested its existence. By citing contemporary astronomers and their speculative theories, and thinking about how they would apply to a voyage to the Moon, Poe gave the concept of spaceflight a new basis in science. In some respects, however, Poe’s insights into the psychological and behavioral characteristics that would lead to spaceflight were even more insightful than his clever applications of contemporary astronomy. Although he is still working within the lone-inventor model employed by Godwin and Tucker, the inventor is no longer an aristocratic adventurer, an extraterrestrial, or a mystic scientist, but rather a simple engineer — Hans Pfaall, an underemployed and debt-ridden Dutch bellows maker in Rotterdam. Even more significantly, this inventor begins to approach the level of single-minded obsession and dedication of effort and resources that would possess many of the early pioneers of spaceflight. items.title: Field Guide to Predators in Their Natural Habitat
items.summary: The Photographs Never Develop Like You Imagine I’m a photographer , he said, I want you to pose for me . A camera dangled from his neck instead of a whistle— otherwise he was my dad’s stand-in, blue Oxford tucked into khakis. He found me in the concession line, five bucks sweating in my palm. My mother was cheering on my twin brother’s soccer team; my father was the coach, and the August heat played goal against an unstoppable dark. He steered me to the swings, pinching my arm, then to the playground horses, their painted-on eyelashes batting. He posed me how he wanted me seen. From the field I heard my brother starting a fist-fight; when I turned to look, the man shook my chin back into place. Don’t move , his voice like cleats scraping knees. He orbited me, excited electron, saliva foaming at the corners of his mouth as he shot. Good girl . I didn’t correct him, his camera glared a gleam. He fixed me atop the jungle gym; when ordered, I hung inverted, Like a Princess transforming into a bat . His lens stiffened from its cave. Shutterstun of clicks. I struggled to right myself. After, he bought a Kit Kat we shared behind the stand. His thumb slid chocolate across my cheek, my last picture. He walked me into view, finger jabbing my spine forward, to where a referee was handing my offsides brother a red card. My mother jotted our address on a used roster. Before he left, he said, You have such a beautiful daughter . In the van, my mother said, Don’t go missing like that . The next day, she shaved my head. I watched the mailbox but nothing ever came. I never saw the girl he took again. Junior Scientist Summer Camp That June we were scientists, bluing liquids in our beakers, iodinating slides to illuminate the interior lives of basil, gluing bisected stamens into our starter field guides. We wore test-tube toolbelts to collect stream samples; I used mine like a sash since it wouldn’t fit my waist. Misty Mills dubbed me Nerd Rambo, but Andrea Gerber’s nickname stuck: Miss Obesity, 1989. I was fixed in their binocular crosshairs after that. Every day, we returned to Maitland Middle School’s laboratories, composition pages full, feeling older, on the brink of discovery. I rode in the back of the bus, self-exiled, my fat body jostling from the rural roads. Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic: I memorized the solid world like an alien trying to learn how he fit in the new ecosystem. Then Jeremy Fradin said, Look at his titties bounce! and the boys circled like white coats in a medical theater, eyes wide as magnifying glasses. I was a specimen, my sweating thighs stuck to the leather seat. Damon Bixler cupped my breasts from behind. Mark Collins lifted my shirt. I sent my mind into the passing orange groves in full fruit. I stayed still while anonymous hands took turns to twist. Like radio dials , a voice as far away as Venus said. I heard the girls giggling from farther galaxies. I practiced reciting in my head: krypton, xenon, boron, argon, neon, the gases once called inert and which we now call noble because of their impenetrable electron shells. items.title: Naturalness: a useful principle, but not an absolute rule
items.summary: There are two classes of problems that physicists often talk about that might leave you thinking, “geez, a physicist can never be satisfied, can they?” The first is called a coincidence problem: where things that have no apparent reason for being close together actually are close together. Examples include: the normal matter and dark matter densities, the cosmic matter density and the dark energy density, the total energy of the Hoyle state of carbon-12 being almost exactly equal to the rest mass energy of three helium-4 nuclei, or Dirac’s large number coincidence , where the strength of gravity is approximately equal to the inverse of the age of the Universe since the Big Bang. The second is the opposite type of problem, known as a hierarchy problem: where it seems like there is a large, unnatural, inexplicable gap between things that — if everything were equal — you might expect to be close together. Examples of that include: the huge differences between the electroweak scale and the Planck scale, the huge difference in the strength between gravity and electromagnetism, the big difference between the mass of most of the massive particles in the Standard Model and the tiny masses of neutrinos, or the cosmological constant problem, arguably the largest-magnitude mismatch of them all. You might think that having both “coincidence” and “hierarchy” problems just means that physicists are always looking for trouble, and can never be satisfied. But both sets of problems are just the extreme poles of fine-tuning, and naturalness is one often (but not always) useful way to approach it. Here’s what the big idea is all about. Explanatory diagram showing how symmetry breaking works. At a high enough energy level, a ball settled in the center (lowest point), and the result has symmetry. At lower energy levels, the center becomes unstable, the ball rolls to a lower point – but in doing so, it settles on an (arbitrary) position and the result is that symmetry is broken – the resulting position is not symmetrical. An outcome that may seem unlikely can be made sense of if the history of the system, and a mechanism that naturally leads to that seemingly unlikely outcome, can be correctly identified. Credit : FT2/Wikimedia Commons The study of the Universe itself — both in terms of the fundamental laws that govern it as well as the ingredients that make it up — is, by definition, the study of nature. Assuming that we, as humans, can intuit what is itself “natural” is kind of a bit of hubris on our part: nature simply is what it is, and we, ourselves a product of nature, can only hope to figure out what it is and how it got to be this way. And yet, it’s been an incredibly successful approach at times. A “natural” idea simply posits the following: When we find two quantities that are close together, but don’t appear to be related, we ask what sort of relationship could exist that would lead to those quantities matching (or nearly matching) one another. And when we find two quantities that we might expect to be close together, but that instead turn out to be very far apart, we ask what sort of mechanism could exist for leading to those quantities having such a severe mismatch in reality. In other words, the idea of naturalness is simply to state that instead of the Universe just being the way it is, full of coincidences, huge disparities, and all sorts of “fine-tunings” that had to occur for it to turn out the way it did, there ought to be mechanisms in place that led to it being the way we observe it to be. Balanced Rock, shown here in photos from before 1975 (black and white) and after 1976 (color), showcases how weathering and erosion can lead to the collapse of structures over time. At right, the structure once known as “Chip off the Old Block” fell during the winter of 1975-1976, and someday, Balanced Rock will fall as well. However, it was created by natural processes, even if it doesn’t appear so; understanding how is the key to solving what appears, on the surface, to be a fine-tuning problem. Credits : National Parks Service/Neal Herbert Throughout the history of theoretical physics, and in particular during the development of the Standard Models of particle physics and cosmology throughout the 20th century, this approach turned out to often be incredibly useful. In the early days of quantum physics, people started asking questions about the electric field that surrounded the electron and how you could reconcile that with a point-like particle, which experiments supported. If you calculated the total electrostatic energy stored in an electric field created by a charged “point,” you’d get a catastrophic answer: an infinite amount of energy. But this isn’t possible; we know that the electron has a finite, observed rest mass, and that therefore the total energy of the electron can be no greater than the value given by E = mc² , where m is the mass of the electron. This puzzle, of the electron’s self-energy , led to the development of a whole new field to get a finite answer rather than the unnatural, infinite one that was classically predicted: quantum field theory . Along with that development came a novel prediction, the existence of an antimatter particle that was oppositely charged to the electron, the positron , and eventually the development of quantum electrodynamics. The so-called ‘Dirac sea’ arose from solving the Dirac equation, based on a complex vector space, which yielded both positive and negative energy solutions. The negative solutions were soon identified with antimatter, and the positron (antielectron) in particular opened up an entire new world for particle physics. Credit : Incnis Mrsi / PUBLIC DOMAIN In nuclear physics, there was a puzzle that arose when it came to the generation of the elements in the Universe: the puzzle of carbon. We were able, even in the 1950s, to easily measure the rest mass energy of the different elements and their isotopes, including: hydrogen (with a single proton as its nucleus), helium (with helium-4, with two protons and two neutrons as its nucleus being the most abundant), and carbon (with carbon-12, with six protons and six neutrons, being the most common version). But if stars were the dominant source of carbon in the Universe, then there was a problem that arose: the mass of carbon-12 was too mismatched, given the properties of the interiors of stars, from the mass of the three helium-4 nuclei, combined, that must go into creating it. So how was carbon made? It was by thinking along this line that Fred Hoyle hypothesized a natural solution to this problem, and a mechanism by which carbon-12 could be created in the necessary abundance: he theorized the existence of a new, excited state for carbon-12 nuclei whose energy was exactly (or almost exactly) equal to the rest mass energy of three helium-4 nuclei combined. This state, the Hoyle state , was later observed by nuclear physicist Willie Fowler, marking a remarkable success for the naturalness approach. If the value of that excited state of carbon-12, which turned out to be a 7.654 MeV resonance, were different in energy by even 5%, our Universe wouldn’t have made the carbon that enabled our existence. The prediction of the Hoyle State, an excited state of a carbon-12 nucleus, and the discovery of the triple-alpha process is perhaps the most stunningly successful use of anthropic reasoning in scientific history. If the mass of the excited state of carbon-12 were even 5% more or less energetic than its value above the ground state, we would make too little carbon to explain the abundance observed in our Universe.
